title: Retry
summary: Retrying failed requests is the simplest reliability pattern — but done wrong, it makes failures worse. Retries must be idempotent, bounded, and use exponential backoff with jitter to avoid retry storms.
why_it_matters: Networks fail. Services fail. Transient errors are normal in distributed systems. Without retries, every transient error becomes a user-facing failure. With naive retries, a brief outage becomes a cascade that takes down the whole system. Retries done right are invisible; done wrong, they're catastrophic.

payload.text:
In a distributed system, transient failures are normal: a network blip, a momentary overload, a rolling deploy. Retrying the request is the natural response — but it must be done carefully.

A naive retry (`if failed, try again immediately`) can make things much worse. If 10,000 clients all retry at once when a service recovers, it goes down again immediately. This is called a **retry storm**.

payload.code:
flowchart LR
  Request[Request] --> Attempt1[Attempt 1]
  Attempt1 -->|transient failure| Backoff[Exponential backoff + jitter]
  Backoff --> Attempt2[Retry]
  Attempt2 -->|success| Done[Success]
  Attempt2 -->|repeated failure| Fail[Fail / fallback]
payload.caption: Retry: apply a pattern to a recurring architectural pressure.

payload.text:
Good retries follow 4 rules:

1. **Only retry idempotent operations.** If the operation might have side effects (POST to /charge), retrying might duplicate the effect. Use idempotency keys to make non-idempotent operations safely retryable.
2. **Exponential backoff.** Wait 100ms, then 200ms, then 400ms, then 800ms. Give the failing service time to recover.
3. **Add jitter.** Add a random component to the delay (e.g., 100ms + random(0-50ms)) so clients don't all retry at the same instant.
4. **Bound the retries.** After 3-5 attempts, give up. Infinite retries can hang the system.

payload.title: Combine with a circuit breaker
payload.body: Retries handle transient failures. But if a service is down for minutes, retrying every request for minutes is wasteful and harmful. A circuit breaker detects sustained failures and stops sending requests entirely — 'trips open' — for a cooldown period, then tests if the service has recovered ('half-open'). See the Circuit Breaker lesson.

payload.text:
Not all errors should be retried:

- **Retry**: 429 Too Many Requests, 500/502/503/504 server errors, network timeouts.
- **Don't retry**: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found. These are client errors — retrying won't fix them.

Most HTTP clients (axios, fetch with wrappers) support configurable retry policies. Use them.

payload.question: Your API client retries failed requests with a fixed 100ms delay. The downstream service goes down for 30 seconds. What happens?
options: The service recovers cleanly when it comes back up.
All clients retry at the same 100ms intervals, causing a thundering herd that may prevent recovery.
The retries have no effect on recovery.
The client gives up after 3 retries.
payload.rationale: A fixed delay (no jitter) means all clients retry at the same intervals. When the service recovers, all clients hit it simultaneously — a thundering herd. This can overwhelm the recovering service and cause it to go down again. The fix is exponential backoff with jitter: each client waits a different, exponentially increasing amount, spreading the load over time.

payload.question: Which HTTP status code should you NOT retry?
options: 503 Service Unavailable
429 Too Many Requests
404 Not Found
502 Bad Gateway
payload.rationale: 404 Not Found is a client error — the resource doesn't exist. Retrying won't make it appear. 503, 429, and 502 are all transient server-side errors that may succeed on retry: 503 means the server is temporarily unavailable, 429 means you're being rate-limited (retry after the delay in the header), and 502 means a bad gateway (the upstream service is unreachable).

payload.text: **Mental model.** Think of Retry as a deliberate boundary in a system. The boundary exists because something becomes harder to manage when everything is done in one place: latency, scale, failure isolation, consistency, cost, or team ownership. The useful question is not “what does Retry mean?” but “what pressure makes this boundary worth introducing, and what new failure mode does it create?”

payload.title: Design lens
payload.body: Before choosing Retry, name the workload, the critical user path, the dominant bottleneck, the failure you are trying to absorb, and the trade-off you are willing to accept. If you cannot name those five things, the design is probably premature.

payload.title: Hint
payload.body: If you are stuck on Retry, start by drawing the request path and marking every network hop, stateful component, queue, cache and failure boundary. Then estimate where the system will saturate.

payload.question: You increase traffic by 10× in a system using Retry. What should you inspect first?
options: The newest framework version
The dominant bottleneck and its saturation signal
Only the UI
Nothing; the architecture should absorb any traffic automatically
payload.rationale: System design is a constraint-and-bottleneck exercise. Start with the resource or dependency that will saturate first, then choose the smallest change that removes that bottleneck.

payload.question: Which statement is the safest engineering habit when using Retry?
options: Choose it because it is popular
Add it before measuring the problem
State the workload, failure mode and trade-off it is solving
Use the most distributed design possible
payload.rationale: Good architecture starts from requirements, workload and failure assumptions. The component is the consequence of that reasoning, not the starting point.

payload.prompt: Production scenario: your system uses Retry, traffic suddenly spikes, and p99 latency doubles. What is your first move?
payload.context: You have dashboards for traffic, latency, errors and saturation. You can change the architecture, but every change has operational cost.

options.outcome: This may help, but only if compute saturation is the bottleneck.

options.text: Inspect the bottleneck and its saturation signal first
options.outcome: Correct: diagnose before scaling or introducing a new pattern.
This removes the evidence you need to diagnose the incident.

payload.rationale: Measure the limiting resource or dependency first. A bottleneck can be compute, database I/O, network, cache misses, lock contention, downstream latency, or queue backlog.

payload.text: **Answer this without notes:** When would you choose Retry, and when would you intentionally avoid it? Mention at least one bottleneck it addresses, one failure mode it introduces, and one alternative. Then quantify the workload you are designing for.

payload.title: Engineering lens
payload.body: For Retry, treat the system as a control loop: observe load and failure, choose a bounded response, and measure whether the response stabilizes the system instead of simply moving the bottleneck somewhere else.

payload.text:
### Numerical sanity check

When estimating capacity, distinguish average from peak. If average traffic is 4,000 RPS and the observed peak-to-average factor is 3×, design the first pass around roughly 12,000 RPS, then leave headroom for failure and growth.

payload.question: What is the earliest signal that Retry is becoming the bottleneck: latency, saturation, errors, queue depth, or something else? Why?
payload.context: Do not optimize for a memorized definition. Reason from the workload and failure mode.
options: Scale the same component immediately.
Measure the current bottleneck and state the assumption that changed.
Add more technologies until throughput improves.
Choose the most popular architecture.
payload.rationale: Good system design starts with the bottleneck and the changed constraint. The most popular or complex choice is not automatically correct.

pros: Transparently handles transient failures — users don't see them.
Simple to implement — most HTTP clients support it.
Improves perceived reliability without infrastructure changes.
cons: Retrying non-idempotent operations can duplicate side effects (double charges).
Naive retries cause thundering herds that prevent recovery.
Retries add latency — a request that retries 3 times takes 3x longer to fail.
Too many retries can cascade — a slow service makes all its callers slow.

failure_modes: Retry storms — all clients retry simultaneously and overwhelm the recovering service.
Retrying non-idempotent operations — duplicates side effects (payments, sends).
Infinite retries — a single failed request hangs forever.
Retrying client errors (4xx) — wastes resources, never succeeds.
common_mistakes: Using a fixed retry delay instead of exponential backoff with jitter.
Retrying every error — including 4xx client errors that will never succeed.
Not bounding the retry count — infinite retries can hang the system.
Forgetting to make operations idempotent before adding retries.
where_you_see_it: Every message queue consumer (retry failed messages).
